settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: By design ESI include src is authored by the page/template owner, so in the common case it is trusted configuration rather than user input; the code provides no attacker-controlled path within the read spans.
The provider prefix branch (PROVIDER{...}) selects a named Driver from DriverFactory rather than an arbitrary host, which limits the purely absolute-URL case to the non-provider form.
No test or config in the read spans demonstrates an untrusted origin for src.
candidates.description: IncludeElement.onTagEnd reads the src and alt attributes of the <esi:include> tag (IncludeElement.java:75-76) and passes them to processPage, which resolves the provider/driver and then calls driver.render(page, ...) (IncludeElement.java:143-157, 204-207). No check in the read code restricts src to a relative URL or to the configured provider host; the alt attribute is used the same way on error (IncludeElement.java:92-103). Downstream, Driver.render builds the target with ResourceUtils.getHttpUrlWithQueryString(resultingPageUrl, driverRequest, false) (Driver.java:163-165) and then issues requestExecutor.execute(outgoingRequest) (Driver.java:179-181). ResourceUtils.getHttpUrlWithQueryString only prepends the driver base URL when the value does NOT start with "http://" or "https://" (ResourceUtils.java:67-74), i.e. an absolute URL supplied in src is passed through unchanged to the HTTP client. In deployments where ESI markup is derived from content that an attacker can influence (a later/upstream provider response, or a reflected page that embeds user input into an ESI include), this would let the aggregator be pointed at arbitrary internal or external hosts (SSRF). This is reported as a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability: the review could not read IncomingRequest/DriverRequest, the surrogate extension, or the ESI renderer entry points, so it is unproven whether src is ever attacker-controlled in a given deployment, and there may be validation elsewhere (e.g. in the parser, in the surrogate extension, or a same-host policy) that was not readable.
missing_evidence: IncomingRequest / DriverRequest and the EsiRenderer/Esi extension entry points that determine whether the parsed body can be attacker-influenced.
Any host allowlist, base-URL pinning, or SSRF guard implemented in classes not readable here (e.g. OutgoingRequest, HttpClientRequestExecutor lines 121-331, extensions).
Whether GetUrlWithQueryString output is re-validated before execute().
preconditions: ESI markup containing an <esi:include src="http(s)://host/..."> is processed by the esi IncludeElement
At least one provider response or template that reaches EsiRenderer contains src content influenced by an untrusted party
No external configuration or extension enforces a host allowlist for ESI includes
candidates.title: ESI include src/alt from parsed content reaches an unrestricted outbound URL builder (potential SSRF)

counter_evidence: The constructor also accepts an XSL string (XsltRenderer.java:84-87); in that path the stylesheet is supplied programmatically, not from untrusted content.
Java's built-in TransformerFactory may already restrict external DTD/stylesheet access by default depending on JDK version, so the risk may be mitigated by the runtime.
No code in the read spans shows a user-controlled origin for the stylesheet.
candidates.description: XsltRenderer declares a static javax.xml.transform.TransformerFactory obtained with TransformerFactory.newInstance() (XsltRenderer.java:57) and builds the stylesheet via TRANSFORMER_FACTORY.newTransformer(new StreamSource(templateStream)) (XsltRenderer.java:89-97). No call setting FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING or the ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD / ACCESS_EXTERNAL_STYLESHEET (JAXP 1.5) attributes appears in the read span, so the effective restriction depends entirely on the JAXP implementation defaults and any system properties. The stylesheet itself comes from the ESI "stylesheet" attribute through IncludeElement.processPage (IncludeElement.java:146, 201-202 -> XsltRenderer.java:70-76), which fetches the template through driver.render; if that attribute can be influenced, or if a fetched stylesheet contains xsl:include/import/document(), the untrusted stylesheet is compiled under whatever external-access policy the default factory allows. Reported as a candidate because the actual reachability of user-controlled stylesheet content and the runtime factory defaults were not verifiable from the readable code.
missing_evidence: The JDK/JAXP implementation and version actually used at runtime, which determines default ACCESS_EXTERNAL_* behavior.
Whether IncludeElement's stylesheet attribute is ever populated from untrusted input (needs the surrogate extension / renderer entry points).
Any global factory configuration performed elsewhere (e.g. by an extension or a system property).
preconditions: An ESI include with a stylesheet attribute is processed, causing XsltRenderer to compile a stylesheet
The stylesheet content can be influenced by an untrusted source (not demonstrated in the read spans)
candidates.title: XSltRenderer uses a default TransformerFactory without visible secure-processing / external-access restrictions

counter_evidence: The XPath is evaluated with the standard JAXP XPath implementation rather than a scripting/reflection engine, and NODESET evaluation is bounded by the parsed document in memory.
No evidence in the read spans that the xpath attribute is attacker-controlled; it is normally template-author supplied.
The document itself is already fully parsed in memory before evaluation, so the marginal cost is bounded by document size.
candidates.description: When an <esi:include> tag carries an xpath attribute, IncludeElement adds a new XpathRenderer(xpath) built directly from the attribute value (IncludeElement.java:145, 199-200). XpathRenderer compiles the string with XPathFactory.newInstance().newXPath().compile(xpath) (XpathRenderer.java:48, 51-58) and evaluates it as a NODESET against the parsed document on every render, iterating all matching nodes (XpathRenderer.java:63-73). The expression is taken verbatim from the tag and no length, complexity, or result-size limit is visible in the read ranges, so a very complex expression or a document with a huge number of matches would be executed in full. Reported as a low-confidence candidate: this is only a potential resource-exhaustion/processing concern and the review could not establish that the xpath attribute ever originates from untrusted input, nor could it observe the parser that produces Tag attributes.
missing_evidence: Whether the ESI xpath attribute can be influenced by untrusted content (needs the ESI/surrogate entry points and parser).
The size of documents processed in typical deployments and whether any upstream limit exists (not readable here).
preconditions: An ESI include tag with an xpath attribute is parsed and rendered
The expression or matched document can be made large/complex by an untrusted party
candidates.title: XPath expression supplied by ESI tag is compiled and evaluated without bounds

counter_evidence: Forwarding the original query string is the documented purpose of proxy mode; the client query is generally expected to reach the provider.
The code explicitly strips the container-added jsessionid before forwarding (ResourceUtils.java:42-50).
URI construction itself is delegated to UriUtils/HTTP client helpers, which may normalize values.
candidates.description: ResourceUtils.buildQueryString extracts the raw query string from the incoming request line (ResourceUtils.java:39-40) and, when proxy mode is enabled, removes only the jsessionid before appending it to the outgoing URL (ResourceUtils.java:41-53); getHttpUrlWithQueryString then concatenates it as "url?" + queryString (ResourceUtils.java:75-80). The extracted query is the client-supplied query string, and the read code performs no normalization or validation of query parameters before they are forwarded to the provider application. This is reported only as a weak candidate for potential parameter/URL injection into the proxied request: within the reviewed span there is no evidence that the value is used for anything more sensitive than forming the provider request, and ServerUtils/UriUtils helper behavior for removing the session id could not be fully verified here.
missing_evidence: The full behavior of UriUtils.getRawQuery and UriUtils.removeSessionId (not readable in the reviewed span).
How downstream provider code and the HTTP client handle the assembled URL (OutgoingRequest, HttpClientRequestExecutor beyond line 120).
preconditions: Proxy mode (proxy == true) is used so the original query string is forwarded
An attacker can submit a query string that the provider application treats specially
candidates.title: Original request query string is forwarded to the provider without re-validation in ResourceUtils
